cards.statement: For false; saved=$?; true, Bash leaves saved holding the failure status from false.
cards.explanation: Saving $? immediately captures false's status in saved. The later true changes the current status while saved retains the captured value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Exit Status

cards.statement: For a script ending true; exit 7, Bash reports the status from the preceding true.
cards.explanation: An explicit argument to exit supplies Bash's exit status. This script reports 7 rather than true's successful status.
cards.misconception: exit uses the preceding command's status even when an explicit status is supplied.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: exit builtin

cards.statement: With value writable, Bash reports failure for value=$(false).
cards.explanation: An assignment-only command uses the last command substitution's status. The failing false therefore makes this assignment report failure.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Simple Command Expansion

cards.statement: For false | true; :, Bash leaves PIPESTATUS holding the earlier pipeline's results.
cards.explanation: The simple command : replaces PIPESTATUS with its own successful status. Read or save pipeline results before executing another command.
cards.misconception: PIPESTATUS retains pipeline results across subsequent simple commands.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: PIPESTATUS

cards.statement: In false && true, Bash takes the list's status from the final written command true.
cards.explanation: The failed false causes && to skip true. The list reports its last executed command's status, which is false's failure.
cards.misconception: An AND list takes its status from the final written command even when that command is skipped.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Lists

cards.statement: Bash reaches printf x when it executes the command list true || false && printf x.
cards.explanation: The && and || list operators share precedence and associate leftward. Bash evaluates true || false before applying && printf x.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Lists

cards.statement: Bash reports success for ! true | true because the last true succeeds.
cards.explanation: The leading ! negates the status of the entire pipeline. Both true commands succeed, so ! true | true yields a failure status.
cards.misconception: A leading ! changes the first command's status rather than the computed pipeline status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

cards.statement: Bash reports success for { false; true; } because true runs last in the group.
cards.explanation: A command group returns its list's status. The final true supplies a successful status for this group.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands

cards.statement: With pipefail disabled, Bash selects false's failure as the result of false | true.
cards.explanation: A pipeline uses its final command's status when pipefail is disabled. The final true makes false | true succeed.
cards.misconception: An earlier pipeline failure determines its status while pipefail is disabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

cards.statement: With pipefail enabled, Bash selects the middle command's status in (exit 7) | (exit 9) | true.
cards.explanation: pipefail selects the rightmost nonzero command status. The middle command supplies 9, the selected failure in this pipeline.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

cards.statement: Immediately after (exit 7) | (exit 9), Bash exposes PIPESTATUS values 7 and 9 in command order.
cards.explanation: PIPESTATUS holds a status for each command in the foreground pipeline. These two commands supply 7 and 9, in pipeline order.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: PIPESTATUS

cards.statement: For (exit 7) & p=$!; wait "$p", Bash makes wait return the successful launch status.
cards.explanation: wait "$p" returns the child's termination status, 7. Launching the asynchronous command reports a separate successful status.
cards.misconception: wait reports an asynchronous command's launch status instead of its completion status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: wait builtin and Lists

cards.statement: With set -u and zero positional parameters, Bash treats "$@" as an unset-parameter error.
cards.explanation: nounset exempts the special parameter @. Bash accepts this expansion even when its positional-parameter list is empty.
cards.misconception: nounset rejects quoted @ when the positional-parameter list is empty.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: nounset

cards.statement: With set -e and an ERR trap, Bash runs the trap for false in if false; then :; fi.
cards.explanation: A failure used as an if condition is exempt from ERR and errexit. Bash completes this if statement with the trap unexecuted.
cards.misconception: An if condition's failed command triggers ERR when errexit is enabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin and trap builtin

cards.statement: With set -e, Bash reaches printf x when it executes false || printf x.
cards.explanation: The nonfinal command in this || list is exempt from errexit. Its failure selects printf x as the recovery command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

cards.statement: With set -e, Bash triggers errexit at ! true in ! true; printf x.
cards.explanation: Bash ignores errexit for a pipeline whose status is inverted with !. This script therefore continues to printf x.
cards.misconception: A negated pipeline's failed overall status triggers errexit.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

cards.statement: With set -e, Bash stops f at false in f(){ false; printf x; }; if f; then :; fi.
cards.explanation: Calling f as an if condition makes Bash ignore errexit throughout that function body. The false is followed by printf x.
cards.misconception: A tested function call retains errexit handling for failures inside its body.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

cards.statement: With set -e -o pipefail, Bash exits before printf x in false | true; printf x.
cards.explanation: pipefail makes this untested pipeline fail. errexit acts on that pipeline status and exits before the following printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit and pipefail

cards.statement: With set -e, Bash exits before printf x when it executes false; printf x.
cards.explanation: The standalone false reports failure in an untested context. errexit ends this shell before it reaches the following command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

cards.statement: With set -e and inherit_errexit enabled, Bash stops before the inner printf in value=$(false; printf x).
cards.explanation: inherit_errexit carries -e into this substitution's subshell. The untested false stops that subshell before its printf command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: shopt builtin: inherit_errexit

cards.statement: With set -e and n=0, Bash exits before printf x in ((n++)); printf x.
cards.explanation: The arithmetic command evaluates n's old value, zero, and returns status 1. errexit stops this untested sequence before printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Commands and set builtin

cards.statement: With set -e, Bash uses false's failure as local's status in f(){ local value=$(false); }; f.
cards.explanation: A valid local declaration returns its own successful status, masking the substitution's failure. errexit therefore continues past local in this call.
cards.misconception: local propagates a command substitution's failure status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: local builtin and set builtin

cards.statement: With set -u and x unset, Bash passes an empty argument to printf '%s' "$x".
cards.explanation: Expanding an unset scalar as "$x" under nounset causes an error. Bash exits before invoking printf.
cards.misconception: nounset converts expansion of an unset scalar into an empty argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: nounset

cards.statement: With set -u and x unset, Bash runs printf '%s' "${x-}" successfully.
cards.explanation: The guarded ${x-} form handles unset x explicitly. Bash accepts that expansion under nounset and executes printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion and set builtin

cards.statement: With cleanup(){ :; }, trap 's=$?; cleanup; exit "$s"' EXIT preserves the pending exit status.
cards.explanation: The EXIT handler captures the pending status before cleanup runs. cleanup returns normally, and the handler finishes with that saved status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap and exit builtins

cards.statement: After trap 'cleanup' EXIT, Bash leaves the EXIT handler installed when trap -p EXIT runs.
cards.explanation: trap -p prints definitions of installed traps for inspection; it leaves those handlers in place.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

cards.statement: After replacing TERM handler 'cleanup' with ':', Bash uses trap - TERM to restore 'cleanup'.
cards.explanation: trap - TERM restores the TERM disposition from when Bash started. It does not undo installed handlers one at a time.
cards.misconception: Resetting a trap restores the previously installed action.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

cards.statement: After trap '' TERM, Bash passes the ignored TERM disposition to external commands it executes.
cards.explanation: An empty trap action makes TERM ignored. External commands launched by Bash start with that ignored disposition.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Signals and trap builtin

cards.statement: When Bash catches TERM while awaiting a foreground external command, it runs its TERM trap before that command ends.
cards.explanation: Bash defers a trap for a signal it catches during foreground waiting until the external command finishes.
cards.misconception: Bash interrupts foreground waiting to execute a caught signal's trap immediately.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Signals

cards.statement: When Bash catches trapped TERM during wait for an asynchronous child, wait returns a status greater than 128.
cards.explanation: A caught signal interrupts wait with a status greater than 128, after which Bash runs its handler.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Signals

cards.statement: Bash runs an installed EXIT trap when the script finishes with status zero.
cards.explanation: Finishing with status zero still terminates the shell, so Bash runs the installed EXIT handler.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

cards.statement: Bash runs an installed DEBUG trap after a top-level simple command executes.
cards.explanation: Bash executes an installed DEBUG action before a top-level simple command runs.
cards.misconception: DEBUG observes a simple command after it has executed.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

cards.statement: Bash runs an installed RETURN trap after a sourced file finishes executing.
cards.explanation: The RETURN event covers completion of a script run by . or source. Bash executes the installed handler as sourcing finishes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

cards.statement: With ERR trapped and errtrace off, Bash fires that trap inside f(){ false; :; } when f runs.
cards.explanation: With errtrace disabled, an ordinary function does not inherit the caller's ERR trap. Enabling errtrace supplies that inheritance.
cards.misconception: An ordinary function inherits its caller's ERR trap while errtrace is disabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errtrace

cards.statement: With functrace disabled, an ordinary untraced function inherits its caller's DEBUG trap.
cards.explanation: An ordinary untraced function does not inherit its caller's DEBUG trap with functrace disabled. Enabling functrace supplies that inheritance.
cards.misconception: An untraced function inherits DEBUG regardless of the functrace setting.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions and set builtin: functrace

cards.statement: Bash runs its EXIT cleanup trap when SIGKILL terminates the shell.
cards.explanation: SIGKILL terminates the process through an uncatchable signal. Bash gets no opportunity to execute an EXIT cleanup handler.
cards.misconception: An EXIT trap runs cleanup even when SIGKILL terminates Bash.

source.title: signal(7): Signal dispositions

cards.statement: With stdout and stderr initially on the terminal, cmd 2>&1 >out sends stderr to the terminal.
cards.explanation: Bash copies stdout's current destination onto stderr before sending stdout to out. The copied stderr destination remains the terminal.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Redirection

cards.statement: Given descriptor 3 open, Bash closes it for cmd in cmd 3>&-.
cards.explanation: A redirection word of - closes the specified descriptor. Thus 3>&- closes descriptor 3 for that command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Duplicating File Descriptors

cards.statement: After successful exec 3>log, Bash restores descriptor 3's previous destination for the next command.
cards.explanation: With no command argument, exec applies its redirections to the current shell. Descriptor 3 stays connected to log for subsequent commands.
cards.misconception: An exec redirection lasts for one command before Bash restores the previous descriptor.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: exec builtin

cards.statement: Bash applies { printf a; printf b; } >out to both printf commands.
cards.explanation: A redirection attached to the brace group applies to its command list. Both printf commands write through the redirected stdout.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands and Redirection

cards.statement: With noclobber enabled and writable regular file out present, : >|out fails because out exists.
cards.explanation: The >| operator overrides noclobber's existing-regular-file protection. The writable file out is opened and truncated.
cards.misconception: noclobber rejects the >| operator when its target is an existing regular file.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Redirecting Output

cards.statement: With targets='one two', Bash opens two output files for : >$targets.
cards.explanation: An ordinary redirection target must expand to one word. $targets produces two words, so Bash reports a redirection error instead of opening files.
cards.misconception: A redirection target with multiple expanded words opens one output file for each word.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Redirection

cards.statement: For <<'END', Bash passes $name in the here-document body as literal text.
cards.explanation: Quoting any part of a here-document delimiter suppresses expansion in its body. Bash provides $name literally to the command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

cards.statement: With marker=END, Bash uses END as the closing delimiter for <<$marker.
cards.explanation: Bash applies quote removal to the delimiter word, rather than parameter expansion. The closing line for <<$marker contains literal $marker.
cards.misconception: Bash expands variables in a here-document delimiter word.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

cards.statement: With name=dev and <<END, Bash removes double quotes from the body line "$name".
cards.explanation: Double quotes within an unquoted here-document body remain input characters. Bash expands $name but keeps the quotes, yielding "dev".
cards.misconception: Double quotes in a here-document body act as quoting syntax and disappear from the input.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

cards.statement: For <<-END, Bash strips leading tab characters from body lines and the delimiter line.
cards.explanation: The <<- form removes leading tabs as Bash reads the body and recognizes its ending delimiter. Leading spaces stay in the input.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

cards.statement: For <<<"text", Bash supplies the word text followed by a newline as standard input.
cards.explanation: A here string appends a newline to the expanded word. The input for <<<"text" is text followed by that newline.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Strings

cards.statement: With value='a b', Bash rejects : <<< $value as an ambiguous redirection.
cards.explanation: Bash expands the here-string word without word splitting. The unquoted $value contributes one string containing a b, so this redirection succeeds.
cards.misconception: An unquoted here-string word is split into separate redirection targets.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Strings
